title: Gun fit basics
summary: Length of pull, comb height, cast, pitch and weight: why a gun has to fit the shooter, whatever their build, and how fit is checked in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

body.html: In clay shooting you do not aim a shotgun like a rifle, you point it. You look at the target, the gun comes up to the cheek and the shot follows almost at once. A rifle has a rear sight that you line up with the front one. A shotgun has no rear sight: your eye does that job. So if the stock does not put your eye in the right place above the barrels, the shot goes where the gun points, not where you look.

Length of pull is the distance from the trigger to the middle of the butt pad. For adults it is often about 36–38 cm (14¼–15 in), and many factory competition guns come at about 37.5 cm (14¾ in). This is only a guide.

A stock that is too long catches on your clothes as you mount the gun and may land on the arm instead of the shoulder. One that is too short lets the thumb of the trigger hand hit your nose under recoil. A stock is shortened, or fitted with a thinner or thicker pad.

Comb height (gun fitters also say 'drop', meaning how far the comb sits below the line of the rib) decides how high your eye sits above the rib. Many Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting shooters like to see a little of the rib in front of the bead. A higher comb moves the point of impact up, a lower one down.

Faces and necks differ a lot, so the comb height that suits one shooter may not suit another. That is why many competition guns have an adjustable comb, which is raised or lowered without remaking the stock.

Cast is a slight sideways bend in the stock, so that the eye sits exactly over the rib. For a right-handed shooter the stock bends to the right (cast off), for a left-hander to the left (cast on). It is a matter of a few millimetres, but without it a gun may keep shooting to one side.

Factory stocks are made to average dimensions, and many shooters are not average. People with shorter arms, a longer neck or a different chest shape often have to reach forward for the grip and crane the neck down to the comb. They also feel more recoil. Often the cause is the gun's dimensions rather than the shooter's strength.

Pitch is the angle at which the end of the stock (the butt) is cut, compared with the barrels. It decides whether the whole butt rests flat on your shoulder or only its top or bottom corner. If the lower corner (the toe) digs into your chest, it hurts; a fitter can change the pitch or turn the toe slightly outwards.
The grip and fore-end must suit the hand. A grip that is too thick is hard to hold with a small hand, and the finger struggles to sit properly on the trigger.

Weight is a compromise. A light gun tires the arms less but pushes harder into the shoulder; a heavier one swings more steadily and recoils more softly but is tiring over a long day. The rules allow guns no larger than 12 gauge, so a 20 gauge is fine; a lighter 12 gauge with lighter cartridges is another option.
Fit also depends on your master eye. If it is on the other side from the shoulder you shoot from, your coach will suggest what to do. How to check it: Master eye and cross-dominance.

Fitting is done by a coach or a gun fitter. Often you fire at a pattern plate from about 15 m (16 yards), to see whether the centre of the pattern matches where you were looking. Some fitters use a try gun with a fully adjustable stock.

Fit changes with you. With experience your stance and mount become more consistent, and thick winter clothing makes the stock effectively longer. So do not buy your first gun by eye or change everything yourself after reading the internet: shoot several guns, then adjust step by step with an expert.

key_points.html: A shotgun is pointed, not aimed. It has no rear sight: your eye is the sight, so the stock must put it in the right place.
Length of pull is the distance from the trigger to the middle of the butt pad.
Comb height moves the point of impact up or down, cast moves it sideways.
Pitch, grip size and weight also matter, whatever your build.
Fitting is done with a coach or a fitter, checked on a plate and changed step by step.

did_you_know.html: A try gun has a stock on hinges and sliders, so a fitter can change its length, height and cast right on the ground, between shots.

quiz.q: Which way is the stock bent for a right-handed shooter?
quiz.explain: For right-handers it is cast off, to the right; for left-handers cast on, to the left.
